claim: SERT (SLC6A4) is a member of the solute carrier-6 (SLC6) family.
source: The transporters for the monoamines serotonin (SERT), dopamine (DAT), and norepinephrine (NET) are members of the solute carrier-6 (SLC6) family (Kristensen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kristensen et al., 2011.

claim: The uptake of substrates by SERT is fueled by the electrochemical gradient of sodium.
source: The uptake of their eponymous substrates is fueled by the electrochemical gradient of sodium; in addition, DAT and NET can harvest the membrane potential, while SERT utilizes the potassium gradient (Bhat et al., 2021c).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bhat et al., 2021c.

claim: SERT utilizes the potassium gradient for substrate uptake.
source: The uptake of their eponymous substrates is fueled by the electrochemical gradient of sodium; in addition, DAT and NET can harvest the membrane potential, while SERT utilizes the potassium gradient (Bhat et al., 2021c).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bhat et al., 2021c.

claim: DAT and NET can harvest the membrane potential for substrate uptake.
source: The uptake of their eponymous substrates is fueled by the electrochemical gradient of sodium; in addition, DAT and NET can harvest the membrane potential, while SERT utilizes the potassium gradient (Bhat et al., 2021c).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bhat et al., 2021c.

claim: SERT, NET, and DAT are closely related transporters.
source: SERT, NET, and DAT are closely related.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text based on established knowledge of transporter families.

claim: Cocaine binds to all three monoamine transporters (SERT, NET, and DAT).
source: Accordingly, their pharmacology shows a continuum from compounds, which bind to all three transporters (e.g., cocaine), to drugs with exquisite selectivity (e.g., selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors [SSRIs]).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text as an example of non-selective binding.

claim: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) show exquisite selectivity for SERT.
source: Accordingly, their pharmacology shows a continuum from compounds, which bind to all three transporters (e.g., cocaine), to drugs with exquisite selectivity (e.g., selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors [SSRIs]).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text as an example of selective binding.

claim: Monoamine transporters are targets for therapeutically relevant drugs such as antidepressants.
source: Monoamine transporters are targets for both, therapeutically relevant drugs (e.g., antidepressants) and for illicit substances.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text based on established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: Monoamine transporters are targets for illicit substances.
source: Monoamine transporters are targets for both, therapeutically relevant drugs (e.g., antidepressants) and for illicit substances.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text based on established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: Inhibitors such as cocaine, tricyclic antidepressants, and SSRIs bind to and block reuptake through monoamine transporters.
source: Inhibitors bind to and block reuptake through the transporter (e.g., cocaine, tricyclic antidepressants, SSRIs).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text based on established pharmacological knowledge.

claim: Exogenous substrates/releasers such as amphetamines induce efflux of endogenous monoamines by switching the transporter into exchange mode.
source: In contrast, exogenous substrates/releasers (e.g., amphetamines) induce efflux of the endogenous monoamine by switching the transporter from the physiological forward transport mode into an exchange mode (Sitte and Freissmuth, 2015; Hasenhuetl et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sitte and Freissmuth, 2015 and Hasenhuetl et al., 2018.

claim: Partial substrates do not elicit reverse transport to the same extent as full releasers.
source: Partial substrates do not elicit reverse transport to the same extent as full releasers (Rothman et al., 2012; Sandtner et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rothman et al., 2012 and Sandtner et al., 2016.

claim: There is a continuum of compounds ranging from full releasers over partial releasers to atypical inhibitors.
source: In fact, there is a continuum, which ranges from full releasers over partial releasers to atypical inhibitors: minor modifications of the amphetamine- or cathinone-based structures suffice to reduce the efficacy of release and to eventually produce atypical inhibitors or allosteric modulators (Sandtner et al., 2016; Niello et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sandtner et al., 2016 and Niello et al., 2019.

claim: Typical inhibitors bind to the outward-facing conformation of monoamine transporters.
source: Typical inhibitors bind to the outward-facing conformation of the monoamine transporters.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text based on established mechanistic understanding.

claim: Atypical inhibitors trap the transporter in distinct conformational states visited during the transport cycle.
source: In contrast, atypical inhibitors trap the transporter in distinct conformational states, which are visited during the transport cycle (Bhat et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bhat et al., 2019.

claim: Numerous disease-associated mutations in neurotransmitter transporters result in misfolding of the protein.
source: Numerous disease-associated mutations have been identified in neurotransmitter transporters, which result in misfolding of the protein (Bhat et al., 2021b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bhat et al., 2021b.

claim: Atypical inhibitors and partial substrates can act as pharmacochaperones and correct folding defects.
source: Atypical inhibitors and partial substrates are of interest, because they can act as pharmacochaperones and correct the folding defect (Bhat et al., 2019; Bhat et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bhat et al., 2019 and Bhat et al., 2017.

claim: ECSI#6 is N-formyl-1,3-bis (3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl)-prop-2-yl-amine.
source: Here, we studied the inhibition of SERT by the amphetamine derivative ECSI#6 [N-formyl-1,3-bis (3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl)-prop-2-yl-amine], which was identified as a synthesis byproduct of 3,4-methylenedioxy-methamphetamine ('ecstasy') (Pifl et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text with a citation to Pifl et al., 2005.

claim: ECSI#6 was identified as a synthesis byproduct of 3,4-methylenedioxy-methamphetamine (ecstasy).
source: Here, we studied the inhibition of SERT by the amphetamine derivative ECSI#6 [N-formyl-1,3-bis (3,4-methylenedioxyphenyl)-prop-2-yl-amine], which was identified as a synthesis byproduct of 3,4-methylenedioxy-methamphetamine ('ecstasy') (Pifl et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pifl et al., 2005.

claim: ECSI#6 is the first reported uncompetitive inhibitor of SERT.
source: Our experiments show that ECSI#6 is, to the best of our knowledge, the first reported uncompetitive inhibitor of SERT.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript showing uncompetitive inhibition kinetics.

claim: Uncompetitive inhibition by ECSI#6 is accounted for by preferential binding to the inward-facing state of SERT.
source: This mode of inhibition was accounted for by preferential binding of ECSI#6 to the inward-facing state.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data and kinetic modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: ECSI#6 acts as a pharmacochaperone by restoring export from the endoplasmic reticulum of the folding-deficient mutant SERT-PG601,602AA.
source: This binding mode predicted a pharmacochaperoning action of ECSI#6, which was confirmed by examining its effect on the folding-deficient mutant SERT-PG601,602AA: preincubation of HEK293 cells with ECSI#6 restored export of SERT-PG601,602AA from the endoplasmic reticulum and substrate transport.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing restoration of ER export and transport function.

claim: ECSI#6 promotes the delivery of SERT-PG601,602AA to the presynaptic specialization of serotonergic neurons in transgenic flies.
source: Similarly, in transgenic flies, the administration of ECSI#6 promoted the delivery of SERT-PG601,602AA to the presynaptic specialization of serotonergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data from transgenic fly studies.

claim: Cocaine blocks SERT uptake of [3H]5-HT with an IC50 of 9.96 µM at 0.1 µM 5-HT.
source: Cocaine blocks SERT uptake of [3H]5-HT with an IC50(0.1) of 9.96 µM (95% CI: 8.7–11.4, Figure 1A, solid blue curve).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake inhibition data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The IC50 of cocaine for SERT inhibition at 1 µM 5-HT is 9.8 µM.
source: The IC50(1) was indistinguishable from IC50(0.1) (Figure 1A, blue dashed curve, IC50=9.8 µM, 95% CI: 7.1–13.6)
evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake inhibition data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The IC50 of cocaine for SERT inhibition at 10 µM 5-HT is 34.6 µM, representing a ~4-fold right shift.
source: while IC50(10) was right shifted by ~4-fold (Figure 1A, blue dotted curve, IC50=34.6 µM, 95% CI: 24.8–48.3).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake inhibition data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The right shift in cocaine IC50 with increasing serotonin is expected and explained by competitive inhibition.
source: This right shift is expected and readily explained; increasing concentrations of unlabeled 5-HT in the uptake inhibition assay inhibits cocaine binding to SERT in a competitive manner.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from established competitive inhibition mechanisms.

claim: Noribogaine blocks substrate uptake of SERT more potently in the presence of unlabeled 5-HT.
source: Noribogaine, on the other hand, blocked substrate uptake of SERT more potently in the presence of unlabeled 5-HT (cf. solid, dashed, and dotted green lines, Figure 1B, IC50(0.1): 5.68 µM [95% CI: 4.36–7.39], IC50(1): 2.39 µM [95% CI: 1.84–3.09], IC50(10): 1.89 µM [95% CI: 1.46–2.44]).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake inhibition data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The left shift in potency of noribogaine in the presence of unlabeled 5-HT is more prominent with ECSI#6.
source: In the presence of unlabeled 5-HT, this left shift in potency was more prominent with ECSI#6 (cf. solid, dashed, and dotted red lines, Figure 1B, IC50(0.1): 440.5 µM [95% CI: 325.8–595.6], IC50(1): 74.14 µM [95% CI: 55.4–99.22], IC50(10): 19.28 µM [95% CI: 13.23–28.09]).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake inhibition data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Noribogaine and ECSI#6 bind to SERT with higher affinity in the presence of substrate.
source: These observations clearly show that noribogaine and ECSI#6 bind to SERT with higher affinity in the presence of a substrate.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental uptake inhibition data.

claim: The mode of binding of noribogaine and ECSI#6 to SERT differs from that of cocaine.
source: Thus, their mode of binding to the transporter differs from that of cocaine.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the different patterns of IC50 shifts observed experimentally.

claim: Addition of 1 or 10 µM 5-HT shifted the displacement curve of ECSI#6 for [3H]citalopram binding to the right.
source: It is evident from Figure 2C that addition of 1 or 10 µM 5-HT shifted the displacement curve of ECSI#6 to the right to an extent which was comparable to that seen with cocaine (Figure 2A) and noribogaine (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental radioligand binding data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Dixon plots allow for differentiating mutually exclusive from mutually non-exclusive binding.
source: Thus, Dixon plots allow for differentiating mutually exclusive from mutually non-exclusive binding, if one inhibitor (i.e., cocaine, noribogaine, or ECSI#6) is examined at a fixed concentration of the second inhibitor (i.e., serotonin) (Segel, 1975)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Segel, 1975.

claim: Binding of serotonin and cocaine to SERT is mutually exclusive.
source: It is evident from Figure 2D–E that the presence of 1 and 10 µM serotonin progressively shifted the (expected) x-intercept for cocaine (Figure 2D), noribogaine (Figure 2E), and ECSI#6 (Figure 2D). Thus, binding of serotonin and one of these three ligands to SERT was mutually exclusive.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental Dixon plot analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Binding of serotonin and noribogaine to SERT is mutually exclusive.
source: It is evident from Figure 2D–E that the presence of 1 and 10 µM serotonin progressively shifted the (expected) x-intercept for cocaine (Figure 2D), noribogaine (Figure 2E), and ECSI#6 (Figure 2D). Thus, binding of serotonin and one of these three ligands to SERT was mutually exclusive.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental Dixon plot analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Binding of serotonin and ECSI#6 to SERT is mutually exclusive.
source: It is evident from Figure 2D–E that the presence of 1 and 10 µM serotonin progressively shifted the (expected) x-intercept for cocaine (Figure 2D), noribogaine (Figure 2E), and ECSI#6 (Figure 2D). Thus, binding of serotonin and one of these three ligands to SERT was mutually exclusive.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental Dixon plot analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: K+ promotes the return step of SERT and drives SERT into the outward-facing state.
source: K+ promotes the return step of SERT and thus drives SERT into the outward-facing state.
evidence: The claim is based on established mechanistic understanding of SERT transport cycle.

claim: Detectable levels of radioligand binding to SERT can be measured in the presence of 120 mM K+.
source: This allows for measuring detectable levels of radioligand binding in the presence of 120 mM K+ (Bhat et al., 2021c; Schicker et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bhat et al., 2021c and Schicker et al., 2012.

claim: Cocaine is substantially less potent (by an order of magnitude) in inhibiting [3H]citalopram binding in the presence of 120 mM KCl than in the presence of 120 mM NaCl.
source: As expected, cocaine was substantially less potent (by an order of magnitude) in inhibiting [3H]citalopram binding in the presence of 120 mM KCl than in the presence of 120 mM NaCl (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental radioligand binding data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cocaine binds more readily to Na+-bound SERT.
source: This indicates that cocaine binds more readily to Na+-bound SERT.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the differential potency in Na+ vs K+ conditions.

claim: The distinct binding preference of cocaine for Na+-bound SERT was not obvious with noribogaine.
source: This distinct binding preference was not obvious with noribogaine (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental radioligand binding data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ECSI#6 is about 10-fold more potent in displacing [3H]citalopram binding in the presence of 120 mM KCl than in the presence of 120 mM NaCl.
source: Importantly and in contrast to cocaine, ECSI#6 was about 10-fold more potent in displacing [3H]citalopram binding in the presence of 120 mM KCl than in the presence of 120 mM NaCl (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental radioligand binding data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: ECSI#6 clearly preferred K+-bound SERT.
source: Thus ECSI#6 clearly preferred K+-bound SERT.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the differential potency in K+ vs Na+ conditions.

claim: Cocaine is a competitive inhibitor of substrate uptake by SERT.
source: Cocaine and noribogaine are competitive and non-competitive inhibitors of substrate uptake by SERT, respectively (Jacobs et al., 2007; Bulling et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jacobs et al., 2007 and Bulling et al., 2012.

claim: Noribogaine is a non-competitive inhibitor of substrate uptake by SERT.
source: Cocaine and noribogaine are competitive and non-competitive inhibitors of substrate uptake by SERT, respectively (Jacobs et al., 2007; Bulling et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jacobs et al., 2007 and Bulling et al., 2012.

claim: Increasing concentrations of ECSI#6 caused a reduction in both KM and VMAX of 5-HT uptake by SERT.
source: This was the case: increasing concentrations of ECSI#6 shifted the saturation hyperbolae for 5-HT uptake (Figure 3C, top) and caused a reduction in both, KM (Figure 3C, middle panel) and VMAX (Figure 3C, bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental saturation kinetics data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Reduction in both KM and VMAX is the hallmark of uncompetitive inhibition.
source: This is the hallmark of uncompetitive inhibition.
evidence: The claim is based on established enzyme kinetics knowledge.

claim: Cocaine causes a progressive increase in KM values with no change in Vmax values.
source: In the presence of 3 μM (blue squares), 10 μM (blue upward triangles), and 30 μM cocaine (blue downward triangles), there was a progressive increase in KM-values (panel D) with KM = 2.2 µM [95% CI, 1.1–3.3], 3.7 µM [95% CI, 1.9–5.5], and 8.1 µM [95% CI, 1.9–5.5], respectively. The inset in panel D shows the same data on a linear abscissa to visualize the linear relation between apparent KM and cocaine concentration. In contrast to the KM values, the Vmax-values remained constant (panel G, VMAX = 118.3 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 117.4–157.3], 121.1 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 105.5–136.8], and 120.1 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 104.6–135.6], respectively).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental saturation kinetics data shown in Figure 3A, D, and G.

claim: Noribogaine does not change KM values but reduces VMAX in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Preincubation with 1 µM (yellow squares), 3 μM (yellow upward triangles), and 10 μM noribogaine (yellow downward triangles) did not change the KM-values (panel E with KM = 2.4 µM [95% CI, 1.4–3.5], KM = 1.9 µM [95% CI, 0.6–3.3], and 2.4 µM [95% CI, 0.6–5.5], respectively). The inset shows the same data on a linear abscissa. The VMAX on the other hand was reduced in a concentration-dependent manner (panel H with VMAX = 82.4 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 69.3–95.4], 39.9 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 30.6–49.2], and 19.5 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 13.9–24.9], respectively).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental saturation kinetics data shown in Figure 3B, E, and H.

claim: ECSI#6 leads to a drop in both KM and VMAX values.
source: Preincubation with 10 μM (red squares), 30 μM (red upward triangles), and 100 μM ECSI#6 (red downward triangles) led to a drop in both, the KM-values (panel F, KM = 1.7 µM [95% CI, 0.5–2.9], 1.1 µM [95% CI, 0.2–1.9], and 0.4 µM [95% CI, 0.0–0.8], respectively; the inset shows the same data on a linear abscissa) and the VMAX-values (panel I, VMAX = 89.5 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 68.5–110.0], 49.9 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 37.5–62.3], and 20.8 pmol min–1 10–6 cells [95% CI, 15.6–26.0], respectively).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental saturation kinetics data shown in Figure 3C, F, and I.

claim: The transport cycle of SERT can be addressed by whole-cell patch clamp recordings.
source: The transport cycle of SERT can be addressed by whole-cell patch clamp recordings; electrophysiological recordings of currents through SERT provide unmatched temporal resolution of ligand and co-substrate binding and unbinding events (Hasenhuetl et al., 2016; Hasenhuetl et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hasenhuetl et al., 2016 and Hasenhuetl et al., 2015.

claim: When challenged with a substrate like 5-HT or amphetamines, SERT carries inward currents comprised of an initial transient peak current and a steady current.
source: When challenged with a substrate like 5-HT or amphetamines, SERT carries inward currents. These are comprised of an initial transient peak current and a steady current.
evidence: The claim is based on established electrophysiological characterization of SERT.

claim: The peak current reflects the initial synchronized movement of substrate and co-substrate through the membrane electric field.
source: The peak current reflects the initial synchronized movement of substrate and co-substrate through the membrane electric field.
evidence: The claim is based on established mechanistic understanding of transporter electrophysiology.

claim: The steady current arises from an uncoupled current and reflects the continuous cycling of the transporter in the forward transport mode.
source: The steady current arises from an uncoupled current; the underlying channel mode is visited from the K+-bound inward-facing state. Thus, the steady current reflects the continuous cycling of the transporter in the forward transport mode (Schicker et al., 2012; Sandtner et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schicker et al., 2012 and Sandtner et al., 2014.

claim: Inhibitors only elicit a minor peak current on application to SERT-expressing cells.
source: In contrast, inhibitors only elicit a minor peak current on application to SERT-expressing cells (Burtscher et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Burtscher et al., 2018.

claim: Cocaine and noribogaine induced transient peak currents, while ECSI#6 failed to do so.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, cocaine and noribogaine induced transient peak currents, while ECSI#6 failed to do so.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the presence of physiological ion gradients and in the absence of substrate, SERT dwells primarily in the outward-facing conformation.
source: In the presence of physiological ion gradients and in the absence of substrate, SERT dwells primarily in the outward-facing conformation.
evidence: The claim is based on established mechanistic understanding of SERT conformational states.

claim: A precondition for a ligand to elicit a peak current is the ability to bind to outward-facing states.
source: A precondition for a ligand to elicit a peak current is, therefore, the ability to bind to outward-facing states.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mechanistic understanding of peak current generation.

claim: The failure of ECSI#6 to produce a peak current is consistent with the interpretation that this compound binds exclusively to inward-facing states.
source: The failure of ECSI#6 to produce a peak current is, thus, consistent with the interpretation that this compound binds exclusively to inward-facing states.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the electrophysiological data.

claim: Cocaine and noribogaine carry a charge while ECSI#6 does not.
source: It should be noted, however, that cocaine and noribogaine carry a charge while ECSI#6 does not.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of the chemical structures of these compounds.

claim: The kapp of cocaine only increased in the very low concentration range and leveled off at about 2 s–1.
source: This was not the case for cocaine (Figure 4C): as shown previously (Bulling et al., 2012), the kapp of cocaine only increased in the very low concentration range and leveled off at about 2 s–1.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4C and supported by citation to Bulling et al., 2012.

claim: The binding of cocaine is limited by the return step from the inward-facing to the outward-facing state, which is the rate-limiting reaction in the transport cycle of SERT.
source: This is expected for a typical inhibitor, which interacts with the outward-facing conformation of SERT, because the binding is limited by the return step from the inward-facing to the outward-facing state. This is the rate-limiting reaction in the transport cycle of SERT (Schicker et al., 2012; Hasenhuetl et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schicker et al., 2012 and Hasenhuetl et al., 2015.

claim: kapp for both noribogaine and ECSI#6 increased in a linear manner as their concentrations were raised.
source: In contrast, kapp for both, noribogaine (Figure 4D) and ECSI#6 (Figure 4E), increased in a linear manner as their concentrations were raised.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: Noribogaine and ECSI#6 bind to the inward-facing conformation of SERT directly.
source: This can only be achieved, if noribogaine and ECSI#6 bind to the inward-facing conformation of SERT directly.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the linear increase in kapp with concentration.

claim: Noribogaine was ~10-fold more potent than ECSI#6 in imposing the block on the substrate-induced current through SERT.
source: Noribogaine was ~10-fold more potent than ECSI#6 in imposing the block on the substrate-induced current through SERT.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental electrophysiological data.

claim: The kon and koff values for noribogaine were 1.7*10^5±1.6*10^4 M–1 s–1 and 1.4±0.3 s–1, respectively.
source: The extracted kon and koff values were 1.7*105±1.6*104 M–1 s–1 and 1.4±0.3 s–1 and 2.1*104±3.5*103 M–1 s–1 and 1.7±0.5 s–1, for noribogaine and for ECSI#6, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental electrophysiological data.

claim: The kon and koff values for ECSI#6 were 2.1*10^4±3.5*10^3 M–1 s–1 and 1.7±0.5 s–1, respectively.
source: The extracted kon and koff values were 1.7*105±1.6*104 M–1 s–1 and 1.4±0.3 s–1 and 2.1*104±3.5*103 M–1 s–1 and 1.7±0.5 s–1, for noribogaine and for ECSI#6, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental electrophysiological data.

claim: The IC50 value of ECSI#6 for blocking serotonin-induced current in the presence of 30 µM 5-HT was approximately 5 µM.
source: A fit of an inhibition curve to the data points yielded an IC50 value of approx. 5 µM.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Pre-application of 100 µM ECSI#6 for 1 s or 3 s did not result in reduction of the peak current amplitude.
source: We chose this time period because it had been sufficient to allow for a full current block in the other protocol (see Figure 4G): the amplitude of the peak current following the pre-application of 100 µM ECSI#6 was essentially identical to the prior control pulse. When we pre-applied 100 µM ECSI#6 for a longer period (i.e., 3 s) the amplitude of the two peak currents also remained the same (cf. lower traces in panel H).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The lack of inhibition by ECSI#6 pre-application indicates that the affinity of ECSI#6 in the absence of 5-HT is low.
source: The lack of inhibition, thus, indicates that the affinity of ECSI#6 in the absence of 5-HT is low.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the electrophysiological data.

claim: When applied from the intracellular side, ECSI#6 did not cause an appreciable current block.
source: Figure 4I shows representative traces of 5-HT-induced currents recorded from SERT-expressing cells in the absence (in blue) and presence of 100 µM ECSI#6 (in red) in the electrode solution: when applied from the intracellular side, ECSI#6 did not cause an appreciable current block.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: In the ER, the folding trajectory of SERT moves through the inward-facing conformation.
source: In the ER, the folding trajectory of SERT moves through the inward-facing conformation (Chiba et al., 2014; Freissmuth et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chiba et al., 2014 and Freissmuth et al., 2017.

claim: Compounds which bind to the inward-facing conformation act as pharmacochaperones and rescue folding-deficient mutants of SERT and DAT.
source: Compounds, which bind to the inward-facing conformation, act as pharmacochaperones: they rescue folding-deficient mutants of SERT and of DAT (Bhat et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bhat et al., 2019.

claim: ECSI#6 was predicted to have pharmacochaperoning activity based on its binding to the K+-bound inward-facing state.
source: Thus, ECSI#6 was predicted to have pharmacochaperoning activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the binding mode of ECSI#6.

claim: SERT-PG601,602AA has a severe folding defect with the bulk of the protein trapped in the ER at an early stage of the SERT folding trajectory.
source: This mutant has a severe folding defect, the bulk of the protein is trapped in the ER at an early stage of the SERT folding trajectory (El-Kasaby et al., 2010; El-Kasaby et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to El-Kasaby et al., 2010 and El-Kasaby et al., 2014.

claim: Only a small fraction of SERT-PG601,602AA reaches the cell surface where it supports substrate uptake.
source: Accordingly, only a small fraction of SERT-PG601,602AA reaches the cell surface, where it supports substrate uptake, but the folding defect can be corrected, if cells are preincubated with noribogaine (Bhat et al., 2021a)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bhat et al., 2021a.

claim: In HEK293 cells expressing SERT-PG601,602AA, substrate uptake was only ~10% of cells expressing wild-type SERT.
source: as shown in Figure 5A, in paired transient transfections, in HEK293 cells expressing SERT-PG601,602AA, substrate uptake was only ~10% of cells expressing wild-type SERT.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Preincubation of HEK293 cells with 30 µM ECSI#6 or noribogaine resulted in appreciable functional rescue of SERT-PG601,602AA, while cocaine was ineffective.
source: If HEK293 cells were preincubated with 30 µM of cocaine, noribogaine or ECSI#6, appreciable functional rescue was observed with ECSI#6 and the reference compound noribogaine; cocaine was ineffective (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The pharmacochaperoning action of ECSI#6 and noribogaine was concentration-dependent and saturable.
source: This pharmacochaperoning action of ECSI#6 and of noribogaine was concentration-dependent and saturable (Figure 5C)
evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Noribogaine was more potent (EC50=0.46 µM) and more efficacious (Emax = 69.5%) than ECSI#6 (EC50=2.9 µM; Emax = 52%) in pharmacochaperoning SERT-PG601,602AA.
source: noribogaine was more potent (EC50=0.46 µM) and more efficacious (Emax = 69.5% of the transport velocity observed in cells expressing wild-type SERT) than ECSI#6 (EC50=2.9 µM; Emax = 52%).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental uptake data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Membrane proteins acquire N-linked core glycans co-translationally in the ER.
source: Membrane proteins acquire N-linked core glycans co-translationally in the ER; in the Golgi apparatus, they incorporate additional sugar moieties to achieve mature glycosylation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of protein glycosylation.

claim: In the Golgi apparatus, membrane proteins incorporate additional sugar moieties to achieve mature glycosylation.
source: Membrane proteins acquire N-linked core glycans co-translationally in the ER; in the Golgi apparatus, they incorporate additional sugar moieties to achieve mature glycosylation.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of protein glycosylation.

claim: The band at approximately 75 kDa corresponds to the ER-resident core-glycosylated species of SERT.
source: Two species were visualized by immunoblotting of whole-cell lysates from cells transiently expressing wild-type SERT (lane 1 in representative blot displayed in Figure 5D): (i) the band at approximately 75 kDa (labeled C) corresponds to the ER-resident core-glycosylated species (El-Kasaby et al., 2010; Bhat et al., 2021a)
evidence: The claim is based on experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D and supported by citations to El-Kasaby et al., 2010 and Bhat et al., 2021a.

claim: A broad smear migrating in the range of 90–110 kDa represents the transporters carrying mature glycans.
source: (ii) a broad smear migrating in the range of 90–110 kDa (labeled M) represents the transporters carrying mature glycans (Freissmuth et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D and supported by a citation to Freissmuth et al., 2017.

claim: Lysates from cells expressing SERT-PG601,602AA show the predominant presence of the core-glycosylated species indicating ER retention.
source: Lysates from cells expressing SERT-PG601,602AA alone show the predominant presence of the core-glycosylated species indicating ER retention (lane 2, Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Treatment of cells expressing SERT-PG601,602AA with noribogaine or ECSI#6 for 24 hr resulted in a concentration-dependent increase in the appearance of the mature glycosylated species.
source: If lysates from cells expressing SERT-PG601,602AA were treated for 24 hr with noribogaine (lanes 4–8 in Figure 5D) or with ECSI#6 (lanes 9–13 in Figure 5D), there was a concentration-dependent increase in the appearance of the mature glycosylated species.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Noribogaine was more potent than ECSI#6 in enhancing the accumulation of mature glycosylated SERT.
source: Noribogaine was more potent than ECSI#6 (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Pretreatment of cells with a saturating concentration of cocaine did not cause any appreciable increase in the SERT species carrying mature glycans.
source: As expected, pretreatment of cells with a saturating concentration of cocaine did not cause any appreciable increase in the SERT species carrying mature glycans (lane 3, Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The upper bands (labeled M) which appeared in cells incubated with ECSI#6 and noribogaine were resistant to deglycosylation by endoglycosidase H.
source: We confirmed the band assignment by enzymatic deglycosylation (Figure 5F): the upper bands (labeled M), which appeared in cells incubated in the presence of ECSI#6 and of norbogaine, were resistant to deglycosylation by endoglycosidase H (which cannot cleave mature glycans).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental enzymatic deglycosylation data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The core-glycosylated species (labeled C) was susceptible to cleavage by endoglycosidase H resulting in the appearance of the deglycosylated band D.
source: In contrast, the core-glycosylated species (labeled C) was susceptible to cleavage by endoglycosidase H resulting in the appearance of the deglycosylated band D.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental enzymatic deglycosylation data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Human SERT and DAT can substitute for their orthologs in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Human SERT and DAT can substitute for their orthologs in Drosophila melanogaster (Kasture et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kasture et al., 2018.

claim: When administered to flies via their food, pharmacochaperones can restore the delivery of folding-deficient mutants of DAT to the presynaptic specializations of dopaminergic neurons in vivo.
source: Previous studies showed that, when administered to flies via their food, pharmacochaperones can restore the delivery of folding-deficient mutants of DAT to the presynaptic specializations of dopaminergic neurons in vivo (Kasture et al., 2016; Asjad et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kasture et al., 2016 and Asjad et al., 2017.

claim: Serotonergic neurons innervate the dorsal fan-shaped body (FB) neuropil in the central brain of D. melanogaster.
source: Serotonergic neurons innervate the dorsal fan-shaped body (FB) neuropil in the central brain of D. melanogaster.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of Drosophila neuroanatomy.

claim: YFP-tagged wild-type human SERT was expressed in the FB6K-type neurons and delivered to the fan-shaped body when placed under the control of TRH-T2A-Gal4.
source: Similarly, when placed under the control of TRH-T2A-Gal4, YFP-tagged wild-type human SERT was expressed in the FB6K-type neurons (Figure 6C') and delivered to the fan-shaped body (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental imaging data shown in Figure 6C and 6C'.

claim: In flies harboring human SERT-PG601,602AA, the transporter was visualized in the soma of FB6K-type neurons but the fan-shaped body was devoid of any specific fluorescence.
source: In contrast, in flies harboring human SERT-PG601,602AA, the transporter was visualized in the soma of FB6K-type neurons (Figure 6F'), but the fan-shaped body was devoid of any specific fluorescence (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental imaging data shown in Figure 6F and 6F'.

claim: Feeding 3-day old male flies expressing human SERT-PG601,602AA with food pellets containing 100 µM ECSI#6 or 100 µM noribogaine for 48 hr resulted in fluorescence accumulation that allowed for delineating the fan-shaped body.
source: However, if 3-day old male flies expressing human SERT-PG601,602AA were fed with food pellets containing 100 µM ECSI#6 or 100 µM noribogaine for 48 hr, fluorescence accumulated to a level, which allowed for delineating the fan-shaped body (Figure 6G and H, respectively).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental imaging data shown in Figure 6G and 6H.

claim: ECSI#6 and noribogaine exerted a pharmacochaperoning action in vivo, which partially restored the delivery of the mutant transporter to the presynaptic territory.
source: This show that ECSI#6 and noribogaine exerted a pharmacochaperoning action in vivo, which partially restored the delivery of the mutant transporter to the presynaptic territory.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental imaging data in flies.

claim: In flies harboring wild-type human SERT, feeding of ECSI#6 and noribogaine did not have any appreciable effect on the level of fluorescence in the fan-shaped body.
source: As expected, in flies harboring wild-type human SERT, feeding of ECSI#6 and noribogaine did not have any appreciable effect on the level of fluorescence in the fan-shaped body (Figure 6D and E, respectively).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental imaging data shown in Figure 6D and 6E.

claim: SERT is arguably the best understood SLC transporter.
source: SERT is arguably the best understood SLC transporter (César-Razquin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to César-Razquin et al., 2015.

claim: Atomic details are available for several conformations of SERT.
source: Atomic details are available for several conformations of SERT (Coleman et al., 2016; Coleman and Gouaux, 2018; Coleman et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Coleman et al., 2016, Coleman and Gouaux, 2018, and Coleman et al., 2019.

claim: The ligand binding pocket and its coupling to the vestibular binding site have been probed by atomic force microscopy, which defined the energy landscape of the binding interaction at the single molecule level.
source: The ligand binding pocket and its coupling to the vestibular binding site have been probed by atomic force microscopy, which defined the energy landscape of the binding interaction at the single molecule level (Wildling et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wildling et al., 2012 and Zhu et al., 2016.

claim: The kinetics of the SERT transport cycle have been extracted from recordings in real time, which also allowed for deducing the cooperativity of substrate and co-substrate binding.
source: The kinetics of its transport cycle have been extracted from recordings in real time, which also allowed for deducing the cooperativity of substrate and co-substrate binding (Bhat et al., 2021c; Hasenhuetl et al., 2019; Bhat et al., 2017; Segel, 1975; Schicker et al., 2012; Sandtner et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Substrate enhanced the ability of ECSI#6 to inhibit transport resulting in a progressive lowering of the IC50 with increasing concentrations of substrate.
source: Substrate enhanced the ability of ECSI#6 to inhibit transport resulting in a progressive lowering of the IC50 with increasing concentrations of substrate.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake inhibition data.

claim: ECSI#6 decreased the KM and the Vmax of SERT for substrate translocation in a reciprocal manner.
source: In a reciprocal manner, ECSI#6 decreased the KM and the Vmax of SERT for substrate translocation.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental saturation kinetics data.

claim: Uncompetitive inhibition is rare.
source: Uncompetitive inhibition is rare (Cornish-Bowden, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cornish-Bowden, 1986.

claim: In enzymes, uncompetitive inhibition requires binding of the inhibitor to the enzyme-substrate complex.
source: In enzymes, uncompetitive inhibition requires binding of the inhibitor to the enzyme-substrate complex (Cornish-Bowden, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cornish-Bowden, 1986.

claim: The kinetic model offered allosteric binding of ECSI#6 to the fully loaded outward-facing transporter (ToNaS) as one possible solution.
source: Accordingly, the kinetic model also offered allosteric binding of ECSI#6 to the fully loaded outward-facing transporter that is, the ternary complex ToNaS of SERT, substrate and sodium – as one possible solution.
evidence: The claim is based on kinetic modeling results.

claim: The simulations showed that ECSI#6 must bind with KD of 1 µM to ToNaS to recapitulate the experimental data.
source: The simulations showed that ECSI#6 must bind with KD of 1 µM to ToNaS to recapitulate the experimental data.
evidence: The claim is based on kinetic modeling results.

claim: In the presence of sub-saturating 5-HT (10 µM), the affinity estimate of ECSI#6 was >30-fold lower than 1 µM.
source: However, in the presence of sub-saturating 5-HT (10 µM), the affinity estimate of ECSI#6 was >30-fold lower ( Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental radioligand binding data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ECSI#6 and serotonin were not bound simultaneously to SERT.
source: It is also evident from our observations that ECSI#6 and serotonin were not bound simultaneously to SERT: raising the serotonin concentration shifted the curves for a displacement of [3H]citalopram by ECSI#6 to the right.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental radioligand binding data.

claim: ECSI#6 binds to the same site as serotonin, albeit in a different mode.
source: Thus, ECSI#6 binds to the same site as serotonin, albeit in a different mode: binding of ECSI#6 was favored in the presence of potassium.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental binding data.

claim: The affinity estimate of ECSI#6 in the presence of potassium was 5 µM.
source: The resulting affinity estimate (5 µM, Figure 2F) was in the range of the KD-values for the inward-facing potassium-bound conformation of SERT TiK required by the kinetic model to recapitulate the experimental data.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental radioligand binding data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The electrophysiological recordings showed that the block of the steady-state, transport-associated current was imposed by ECSI#6 upon binding to an inward-facing state of SERT.
source: The electrophysiological recordings showed that the block of the steady-state, transport-associated current was imposed by ECSI#6 upon binding to an inward-facing state of SERT.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental electrophysiological data.

claim: In ligand-gated ion channels, uncompetitive inhibition is observed with open channel blockers.
source: In ligand-gated ion channels, uncompetitive inhibition is observed with open channel blockers.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of ion channel pharmacology.

claim: Dizocilpine maleate/MK-801, memantine, ketamine, and related compounds require the presence of agonists to reach their binding site and establish blockage of the NMDA-receptor channel.
source: This is exemplified by the NMDA-receptor, where dizocilpine maleate/MK-801, memantine, ketamine, and related compounds require the presence of agonists to reach their binding site and to establish blockage of the channel (Traynelis et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Traynelis et al., 2010.

claim: Serotonin is required to drive SERT into the transport cycle, where SERT accumulates in the inward-facing state.
source: Serotonin is required to drive SERT into the transport cycle, where SERT accumulates in the inward-facing state, because the return step (TiK → ToK, Figure 7A) is rate-limiting (Schicker et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schicker et al., 2012.

claim: The return step (TiK → ToK) is rate-limiting in the SERT transport cycle.
source: Serotonin is required to drive SERT into the transport cycle, where SERT accumulates in the inward-facing state, because the return step (TiK → ToK, Figure 7A) is rate-limiting (Schicker et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schicker et al., 2012.

claim: The inhibitory action of ECSI#6 is use-dependent, that is, enhanced by substrate.
source: This causes the inhibitory action of ECSI#6 to be use-dependent, that is, enhanced by substrate.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the mechanistic understanding and experimental data.

claim: Preferential binding of ECSI#6 to the potassium-bound, inward-facing state of SERT (TiK) is sufficient to account for all experimental data.
source: Thus, preferential binding of ECSI#6 to the potassium-bound, inward-facing state of SERT (TiK) is sufficient to account for all experimental data.
evidence: The claim is based on integration of experimental data and kinetic modeling.

claim: Ibogaine and noribogaine have been classified as non-competitive inhibitors.
source: Ibogaine and its more potent analog noribogaine have been classified as non-competitive inhibitors.
evidence: The claim is based on established pharmacological classification.

claim: The non-competitive mode of inhibition by ibogaine and noribogaine was attributed to their trapping the transporter in the inward-facing conformation.
source: This mode of inhibition was attributed to their trapping the transporter in the inward-facing conformation (Jacobs et al., 2007; Korkhov et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jacobs et al., 2007 and Korkhov et al., 2006.

claim: The structure of the complex of ibogaine and SERT reveals an inward-facing conformation.
source: In fact, the structure of the complex of ibogaine and SERT reveals an inward-facing conformation (Coleman et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Coleman et al., 2019.

claim: Ibogaine binds to SERT from the extracellular side and cannot gain access to SERT via the inner vestibule.
source: Surprisingly, however, ibogaine binds to SERT from the extracellular side; it cannot gain access to SERT via the inner vestibule (Burtscher et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Burtscher et al., 2018.

claim: Ibogaine and carbamazepine can be bound concomitantly to SERT.
source: Access from the extracellular side also explains, why ibogaine and carbamazepine, which binds to the vestibular (S2) site, can be bound concomitantly (Sarker et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sarker et al., 2010.

claim: An interaction of noribogaine with both the sodium-bound, outward-facing state (ToNa) and the potassium-bound, inward-facing state (TiK) of SERT was required to recapitulate the experimental observations.
source: the kinetic model showed that an interaction of noribogaine with both, the sodium-bound, outward-facing state (ToNa) and the potassium-bound, inward-facing state (TiK) of SERT, was required to recapitulate the experimental observations.
evidence: The claim is based on kinetic modeling results.

claim: The kinetic model revealed a predicted uncompetitive component for noribogaine, which was too small to be detectable in the experimental noise.
source: The kinetic model also revealed the predicted uncompetitive component, which was, however, too small to be detectable in the experimental noise.
evidence: The claim is based on kinetic modeling results.

claim: The overall KM of substrate transport is a compound parameter affected by both the rates of individual partial reactions and the occupancy of individual states in the transport cycle.
source: It is worth pointing out that the overall KM of substrate transport is a compound parameter, which is affected by both, the rates of individual partial reactions and the occupancy of the individual states in the transport cycle (Schicker et al., 2021; Schicker et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schicker et al., 2021 and Schicker et al., 2022.

claim: Noribogaine has a mixed binding mode in contrast to ECSI#6.
source: Based on the insights provided by the combination of experimental observations and kinetic modeling, we conclude that, in contrast to ECSI#6, noribogaine has a mixed binding mode.
evidence: The claim is based on integration of experimental data and kinetic modeling.

claim: The outward- and the inward-facing conformation are equivalent stable folds representing the endpoint of the folding trajectory of a protein.
source: The endpoint of the folding trajectory of a protein is a minimum energy conformation. The outward- and the inward-facing conformation are equivalent stable folds (Ponleitner et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ponleitner et al., 2022.

claim: The ionic conditions in the ER differ from those at the cell surface.
source: The ionic conditions in the ER differ from those at the cell surface.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of cellular physiology.

claim: The absence of a sodium gradient in the ER favors the inward-facing conformation of SERT and other SLC6 transporters.
source: The absence of a sodium gradient favors the inward-facing conformation of SERT and other SLC6 transporters.
evidence: The claim is based on established mechanistic understanding.

claim: It is reasonable to posit that the folding trajectory of SERT and other SLC6 transporters visits the inward-facing conformation.
source: Thus, it is reasonable to posit that their folding trajectory visits the inward-facing conformation (Chiba et al., 2014; Freissmuth et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chiba et al., 2014 and Freissmuth et al., 2017.

claim: Mutations which trap SERT in the inward-facing state act as second site suppressors and restore export from the ER and cell surface delivery of folding-deficient mutants.
source: This conjecture is supported by the observation that mutations, which trap SERT in the inward-facing state, act as second site suppressors: they restore export from the ER and cell surface delivery of folding-deficient mutants (Koban et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Koban et al., 2015.

claim: Many compounds which act as pharmacochaperones on SERT or DAT are atypical inhibitors with appreciable affinity for the inward-facing state.
source: In addition, many compounds, which act as pharmacochaperones on SERT or DAT, are atypical inhibitors with appreciable affinity for the inward-facing state (Bhat et al., 2019; Bhat et al., 2021b; El-Kasaby et al., 2010; Bhat et al., 2021a; Kasture et al., 2016; Asjad et al., 2017; Beerepoot et al., 2016; Sutton et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Noribogaine was more efficacious as a pharmacochaperone than ECSI#6.
source: We note, though, that noribogaine was more efficacious as a pharmacochaperone: Emax of pharmacochaperoning, that is, the extent to which substrate transport was restored at saturating concentrations – was consistently higher with noribogaine than with ECSI#6.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental uptake data.

claim: Variable efficacy of pharmacochaperones was noted previously.
source: Variable efficacy of pharmacochaperones was noted previously (Bhat et al., 2021a; Sutton et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bhat et al., 2021a and Sutton et al., 2022.

claim: Individual mutants are stalled at different positions within the energy landscape of the folding trajectory.
source: Efficacy also depends on the nature of the mutation: individual mutants are stalled at different positions within the energy landscape of the folding trajectory (Freissmuth et al., 2017; El-Kasaby et al., 2010; El-Kasaby et al., 2014; Koban et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Individual mutants must differ in their susceptibility to pharmacochaperoning.
source: Thus, individual mutants must differ in their susceptibility to pharmacochaperoning.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the variable stalling positions in the folding trajectory.

claim: In a given folding-deficient mutant, closely related compounds differ in Emax of pharmacochaperoning.
source: In addition, in a given folding-deficient mutant, closely related compounds differ in Emax of pharmacochaperoning (Bhat et al., 2017; Bhat et al., 2021a; Sutton et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bhat et al., 2017, Bhat et al., 2021a, and Sutton et al., 2022.

claim: Pharmacochaperoning efficacy is an intrinsic property of a compound linked to its chemical structure.
source: Thus, pharmacochaperoning efficacy is also an intrinsic property of a compound linked to its chemical structure.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that closely related compounds differ in efficacy.

claim: There are four mechanisms which account for pharmacochaperoning: binding to and stabilization of the folded state, binding to folding intermediates, prevention of aggregate formation, and dissolution of aggregates.
source: There are four mechanisms, which account for pharmacochaperoning (Marinko et al., 2019): (i) binding to and stabilization of the folded state shifts the folding equilibrium and prevents the backward reaction; (ii) binding to folding intermediates smoothens the energy landscape and precludes stalling of the trajectory in unproductive traps of local minima; (iii) prevention of aggregate formation; and (iv) dissolution of aggregates can maintain or restore the folded state.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marinko et al., 2019.

claim: Misfolded SERT does not form aggregates in the ER.
source: The latter two mechanisms are immaterial to SERT: misfolded SERT does not form aggregates in the ER (Anderluh et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Anderluh et al., 2014.

claim: The EC50 of ECSI#6 for pharmacochaperoning was lower than the concentration required for half-maximum inhibition of substrate uptake at saturating substrate.
source: The EC50 of ECSI#6 for pharmacochaperoning was lower than the concentration required for half-maximum inhibition of substrate uptake at saturating substrate.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental data.

claim: The lower EC50 for pharmacochaperoning than for transport inhibition is circumstantial evidence for an action of ECSI#6 on folding intermediates.
source: This is circumstantial evidence for an action of ECSI#6 on folding intermediates.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of EC50 values.

claim: ECSI#6 is an attractive starting point to search for more efficacious compounds with pharmacochaperoning activity because it is more potent a pharmacochaperone than a transport inhibitor.
source: Regardless of the underlying mechanism, because ECSI#6 was more potent a pharmacochaperone than a transport inhibitor, it is an attractive starting point to search for more efficacious compounds with pharmacochaperoning activity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing differential potency.

claim: In vivo, the action of ECSI#6 on serotonergic transmission is likely to differ from typical competitive inhibitors due to its uncompetitive mode of inhibition.
source: In addition, in vivo, the action of ECSI#6 on serotonergic transmission is likely to differ from typical competitive inhibitors: because of the uncompetitive mode of its inhibition, ECSI#6 is predicted to cause a use-dependent block of SERT.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about in vivo effects based on the mechanism of action.

claim: ECSI#6 is predicted to cause a use-dependent block of SERT.
source: because of the uncompetitive mode of its inhibition, ECSI#6 is predicted to cause a use-dependent block of SERT.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the uncompetitive mechanism.

claim: Serotonergic pathways which are activated are more susceptible to modulation by ECSI#6.
source: Serotonergic pathways, which when activated, are more susceptible to modulation by ECSI#6.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about pathway-specific effects based on use-dependent inhibition.

claim: The ratio IC50(0.1)/IC50(10) for ECSI#6 was 20.6 in the kinetic model simulations.
source: We extracted from these simulations the IC50-values for uptake inhibition by ECSI#6 in the presence of 0.1 and 10 μM 5-HT: the ratio IC50(0.1)/IC50(10) was 20.6, which is reasonably close to the shift of 17.2 observed in Figure 1D.
evidence: The claim is based on kinetic modeling results.

claim: The ratio IC50(0.1)/IC50(10) of 20.6 matches the ratio of occupancy of the TiK state at 10 and 0.1 μM 5-HT.
source: This value matches the ratio of occupancy of the TiK state at 10 and 0.1 μM 5-HT (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is based on kinetic modeling results shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Increasing 5-HT concentrations raise the availability of SERT in the TiK state, which accounts for the enhanced ability of ECSI#6 to block 5-HT transport.
source: Thus, increasing 5-HT concentrations raise the availability of SERT in the TiK state and this – rather than the affinity of ECSI#6 – accounts for the enhanced ability of ECSI#6 to block 5-HT transport.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from kinetic modeling results.

claim: A variation of the KD of ECSI#6 for TiK over three orders of magnitude did not alter the IC50(0.1)/IC50(10) ratio.
source: This interpretation was further substantiated by simulations, where the affinity of ECSI#6 to the TiK state was varied: a variation of the KD over three orders of magnitude did not alter the IC50(0.1)/IC50(10) ratio (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is based on kinetic modeling results shown in Figure 7E.

claim: A KD of 12 µM for ECSI#6 binding to TiK sufficed to reproduce all experimental data.
source: We estimated the binding affinity of ECSI#6 for TiK from the synthetic data (Figure 7G): a KD of 12 µM sufficed to reproduce all experimental data.
evidence: The claim is based on kinetic modeling results shown in Figure 7G.

claim: If KD for ToNa is assumed to be 10 times larger than the KD for TiK, the kinetic model simulations yield an IC50(0.1)/IC50(10) ratio of 5 for noribogaine.
source: If KD for ToNa is assumed to be 10 times larger than the KD for TiK, the kinetic model simulations yield an IC50(0.1)/IC50(10) ratio of 5 for noribogaine.
evidence: The claim is based on kinetic modeling results.

claim: The ratio IC50(0.1)/IC50(10) of 5 for noribogaine is reasonably close to the ratio of 3 observed in actual experiments.
source: This ratio is reasonably close to the ratio of 3, which was observed in the actual experiments.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of modeling results with experimental data.

claim: For ECSI#6 to achieve an IC50(0.1)/IC50(10) ratio of 17–21, the KD(ToNa) must be 100- to 1000-fold larger than KD(TiK).
source: We also systematically varied the ratio of KD(ToNa)/KD(TiK) to examine the ratio required to reach a ratio IC50(0.1)/IC50(10) of 17–21, that is, the range seen with ECSI#6. As evident from Figure 7I, the KD(ToNa) must be 100- to 1000-fold larger than KD(TiK).
evidence: The claim is based on kinetic modeling results shown in Figure 7I.

claim: ECSI#6 has a much higher preference for binding to TiK than noribogaine.
source: Hence, based on these calculations, it is appropriate to conclude that ECSI#6 has a much higher preference for binding to TiK than noribogaine.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from kinetic modeling results.

claim: The simulations of substrate transport in the presence of ECSI#6 recapitulated the reduction in the KM and Vmax of 5-HT transport by SERT.
source: In contrast, the simulations of substrate transport in the presence of ECSI#6 recapitulated the reduction in the KM and Vmax of 5-HT transport by SERT (Figure 8B and D), which was seen in the actual experiments summarized in Figure 3C, F and I, and thus confirmed the uncompetitive mode SERT of inhibition.
evidence: The claim is based on kinetic modeling results shown in Figure 8B and D compared with experimental data.
